items.text: People confuse knowing the concept with knowing the actual interface, understanding "what a CRM does" is not the same as running one daily.

items.heading: IT Is Invisible Until IT
items.text: IT Is Invisible Until It is invisible until you are in a real conversation with someone in the field, no course lists "the unwritten context" as a module.

items.heading: A Skills Gap Analysis Only
items.text: A skills gap analysis only means something when it is run against real evidence, not your own guess about what the new field probably needs. The reliable method is to build your gap list from actual job postings, not from a course provider's syllabus or a generic "top skills for X" article.

items.heading: Step 1, Collect 15
items.text: Step 1, Collect 15 to 20 real job descriptions for the exact role and level you are targeting, from job boards, company career pages, and LinkedIn. Do not stop at three; a small sample makes one unusual posting look like a universal requirement.

items.heading: Step 2, Extract Every Skill,
items.text: Step 2, Extract every skill, tool, and qualification mentioned and count how often each one repeats across the postings. A skill that appears in 15 of 20 listings is a real requirement. A skill that appears once is likely posting-specific noise.

items.heading: Step 3, Sort Each Recurring
items.text: Step 3, Sort each recurring item into transferable or role-specific using the split above, and mark which ones you can already demonstrate, which you partly have, and which are genuinely new.

items.heading: Step 4, Talk to Two
items.text: Step 4, Talk to two or three people already doing the job. Job descriptions describe what companies ask for; people already in the role tell you what actually gets used day to day, which is often narrower and more specific than the posting suggests.
